query: Casting is the predominant fabrication method for high-entropy alloys, but solidification-related porosity and microstructural nonuniformity can cause heterogeneous properties. Studies of other high-entropy-alloy compositions have reported high hardness and notable compressive performance, yet these findings do not establish how to improve CoCrFeNiTi; moreover, some investigated alloys were brittle at 25 °C and displayed only limited plastic deformation at 600 °C. For equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with a simple crystal structure, favorable plasticity and machinability, but low hardness and load-bearing capability, what single intervention could improve hardness and mechanical performance while preserving those favorable characteristics and clarifying the relationship between microstructure and deformation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, a quantitative prediction relative to the unmodified alloy, the processing and testing boundaries within which it should apply, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled microstructural and mechanical experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Improving hardness and mechanical performance of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy while preserving favorable plasticity and machinability can be achieved through a single intervention of adding a specific amount of a refractory element such as tungsten (W) to the alloy composition.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy with a simple crystal structure.
generation.intervention: Adding a specific amount of tungsten (W) to the alloy composition.
generation.conditions: The alloy is processed and tested within the boundaries of high-temperature annealing and uniaxial compression at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The addition of tungsten (W) refines the grain structure and increases the lattice distortion, leading to improved hardness and mechanical performance.
generation.mechanism: The improved hardness and mechanical performance are due to the combined effects of grain boundary strengthening and lattice distortion caused by the addition of tungsten (W).
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy is expected to exhibit a 20% increase in hardness and a 15% increase in compressive yield strength compared to the unmodified alloy, while maintaining favorable plasticity and machinability.
generation.baseline: The unmodified equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy.
generation.boundary: The processing and testing boundaries include high-temperature annealing and uniaxial compression at room temperature.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the optimal amount of tungsten (W) to be added and the potential effects on the alloy's microstructure and mechanical properties.
generation.falsification_experiment: A controlled microstructural and mechanical experiment can be designed to falsify the hypothesis by comparing the microstructure and mechanical properties of the modified alloy with the unmodified alloy. If the modified alloy does not exhibit the predicted improvements in hardness and mechanical performance, the hypothesis can be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractIn order to explore the effect of alloying on the microstructures and mechanical properties of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 at.% V, Mo, and B were added to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy in this work. The effects of the elements and contents on the phase composition, microstructures, mechanical properties, and fracture mechanism were investigated. The results showed that the crystal structures of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs remained unchanged, and the alloys were still composed of FCC and BCC structures, whose content varied with the addition of alloying elements. After alloying, the aggregation of Co, Cr, Al, and Ni elements remained unchanged, and the V and Mo were distributed in both dendritic and interdendritic phases. The tensile strengths of the alloys all exceeded 1000 MPa when the V and Mo elements were added, and the Mo0.2 alloy had the highest tensile strength, of 1346.3 MPa, and fracture elongation, of 24.6%. The alloys with the addition of V and Mo elements showed a mixed ductile and brittle fracture, while the B-containing alloy presented a cleavage fracture.
